paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between what the lambda parameter is intended to do and what existing off-policy learning algorithms actually do. In on-policy methods, lambda moves learning from bootstrapping, which uses current value estimates, toward Monte Carlo learning, which uses experienced returns. Existing off-policy methods interrupt this progression by bootstrapping whenever an exploratory action occurs, even when lambda equals one.

The authors introduce PQ(lambda), a version of Q(lambda) designed to restore the Monte Carlo endpoint. Its central challenge is handling updates already made before an action departs from the target policy. The method can effectively undo the appropriate earlier updates without substantially increasing algorithmic complexity.

The derivation is also a contribution. The authors extend forward-view and backward-view reasoning so that the correspondence applies at each time step, rather than only after an episode ends. They first derive an off-policy prediction method, PTD(lambda), and then PQ(lambda). This supplies a way to reason about online updates while preserving the intended relationship between bootstrapping and Monte Carlo learning.
icml-2014-a-new-q-lambda-with-interim-fo.tldr: PQ(lambda) restores the Monte Carlo endpoint of off-policy Q(lambda) through a derivation that accounts for updates at every time step.

paragraphs: This paper examines two choices that strongly affect L1-Regularized Approximate Linear Programming, or RALP: how states are weighted in its objective and how training samples are distributed. RALP approximates the optimal value function from off-policy samples. Its usefulness therefore depends not just on the approximation method, but also on which parts of the decision problem receive emphasis and data.

State-relevance weights determine the emphasis placed on different states within the linear program's objective. The sampling distribution determines where the information used to build the approximation comes from. The authors investigate how these choices affect approximation quality, using theoretical arguments together with experimental illustrations.

The contribution is an explanation of consequential design decisions within RALP. The results also offer intuition about which Markov decision problems are particularly suitable for this approach. This matters because choosing a regularization method alone does not settle how to construct an effective approximation: the objective's priorities and the data's coverage also shape the result.
icml-2014-an-analysis-of-state-relevance.tldr: The paper explains how state weights and sampling distributions shape RALP's value-function approximation quality.

paragraphs: The authors develop a parallel stochastic coordinate descent method for smooth optimization problems. Coordinate descent updates selected variables rather than treating the entire variable vector as one update. The asynchronous design allows parallel work without requiring all processors to advance together. The method covers unconstrained problems and problems whose constraints separate across coordinates.

Its convergence guarantees depend on the objective's structure. For functions satisfying an essential strong convexity property, the method has a linear convergence rate. For general convex functions, the stated rate is proportional to one divided by the number of iterations. These are distinct guarantees rather than a single rate applying to every smooth objective.

The analysis also connects useful parallelism to the number of variables, n. Near-linear speedup can be expected when processor counts are O(n^1/2) for unconstrained problems and O(n^1/4) for separably constrained problems. The paper includes implementation results on 40-core processors. Together, these contributions describe both convergence behavior and conditions under which adding processors can be productive.
icml-2014-an-asynchronous-parallel-stoch.tldr: An asynchronous coordinate descent method combines conditional convergence guarantees with bounds on processor counts that support near-linear speedup.

paragraphs: The paper combines Bayesian modeling and max-margin learning for problems involving multiple tasks. Max-margin methods supply a discriminative learning objective, while Bayesian methods offer ways to incorporate prior information. Bringing them together allows the learning framework to use both kinds of structure when fitting related prediction tasks.

The framework also supports nonparametric Bayesian feature learning, in which the dimensionality of the latent representation is resolved from data. A computational obstacle is the hinge loss, whose non-smooth form complicates inference. The authors use data augmentation to develop Gibbs sampling algorithms that can handle this loss within the Bayesian formulation.

For the nonparametric models, the proposed algorithms avoid mean-field assumptions and truncated approximations. This is a specific feature of their inference approach, alongside the ability to infer latent dimensionality. Experiments cover both multi-task classification and regression, with reported performance above the evaluated competitors. The findings support the practical value of combining margin-based prediction with flexible Bayesian representations in those tested settings.
icml-2014-bayesian-max-margin-multi-task.tldr: The paper combines Bayesian flexibility with max-margin multi-task learning using data augmentation and Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether a family of causal inference methods can reliably recover causal direction as more sample data become available. These methods operate under the Additive Noise Model. The focus is statistical consistency: whether the inference procedure converges toward the correct direction with increasing data under appropriate conditions.

This question differs from establishing the soundness of the underlying model. A model can provide a basis for distinguishing causal directions, while a procedure that estimates the relevant quantities from samples still needs its own justification. The authors identify this sample-based step as an issue that had received comparatively little attention.

Their contribution is a set of general conditions sufficient for consistency within the studied family of methods. The analysis takes place in a nonparametric setting, so the result concerns inference beyond a fixed finite-dimensional model specification. Its significance is to connect the causal modeling framework with the behavior of actual statistical procedures. The guarantee remains conditional on the derived conditions; it does not assert reliable causal discovery from arbitrary observational data.
icml-2014-consistency-of-causal-inferenc.tldr: The paper derives conditions under which additive-noise causal inference methods consistently recover causal direction from samples.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether high-dimensional linear regression really needs computationally elaborate estimators to achieve strong statistical guarantees. The setting includes structural constraints on the regression parameters. Established approaches solve regularized convex optimization problems, which are tractable in a formal sense but can still become expensive at very large scales.

The authors tackle this cost by changing the estimator itself. They construct variants of ridge regression and ordinary least squares, seeking simpler estimators that may admit closed-form computation. Their central result is that these alternatives can retain statistical guarantees comparable to those of regularized likelihood estimators in the high-dimensional setting.

This shifts attention from accelerating an existing optimization procedure to choosing a statistically justified procedure that is simpler to compute. The paper analyzes the proposed estimators and provides empirical support using simulated data and real microarray data. The stated findings support the possibility of combining simpler estimation with comparable guarantees, rather than assuming that a more involved convex program is always required for structurally constrained regression.
icml-2014-elementary-estimators-for-high.tldr: Variants of ridge regression and ordinary least squares offer simpler high-dimensional estimators with guarantees comparable to regularized likelihood methods.

paragraphs: The paper considers estimating parameters defined as averages of feature functions, including covariance matrices. It focuses on high-dimensional settings where the number of variables may exceed the number of samples. Structural constraints then become part of the estimation problem, such as the sparsity highlighted in covariance estimation.

A key finding is that familiar regularization does not automatically produce a convex optimization problem here. The authors show that regularized maximum likelihood formulations and natural Dantzig variants for covariance estimation are non-convex even when their regularizers are convex. The same issue extends to the broader structured-moment setting, including moments associated with exponential families.

The proposed alternative is a family of elementary convex estimators, many of which have closed-form solutions. A unified statistical analysis treats these estimators within one framework. Applications to climatology and biology data demonstrate their use in real problems. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why standard formulations can be difficult with an alternative that makes computation simpler while retaining a basis for statistical analysis.
icml-2014-elementary-estimators-for-spar.tldr: Elementary convex estimators provide an alternative to non-convex regularized formulations for covariance matrices and other structured moments.

paragraphs: The paper presents an optimizer for objectives written as sums of functions. It aims to combine the inexpensive updates of stochastic gradient descent with the curvature information used by quasi-Newton methods. Each update evaluates only one contributing function or minibatch, while an approximate inverse Hessian scales the update.

The distinguishing idea is to maintain a separate Hessian approximation for each function in the sum. Earlier stochastic second-order approaches treated an individual function's Hessian as a noisy estimate of the whole objective's Hessian. Here, each component's curvature is itself a target for estimation. The resulting quadratic approximations are stored and manipulated within a shared low-dimensional subspace that evolves over time.

That shared representation is intended to control memory and computational demands even when the original optimization space is large. The method requires little or no hyperparameter adjustment, according to the abstract. Experiments report improved convergence across seven diverse optimization problems, and implementations are released in Python and MATLAB. These findings support the proposed combination of component-level curvature modeling and inexpensive incremental evaluation.
icml-2014-fast-large-scale-optimization-.tldr: The optimizer combines inexpensive stochastic updates with separate component-level curvature estimates stored in a shared evolving subspace.

paragraphs: When several annotators label the same data, disagreement may reflect differences in expertise. Simply taking the majority label can ignore those differences and produce a flawed learning model. This paper extends Gaussian process classification to account for multiple annotators whose expertise levels vary.

Gaussian processes provide a framework for representing uncertainty explicitly. The proposed extension uses that framework to model the multiple-annotator setting instead of treating every annotation as equally informative. The central motivation is that learning should account for who supplied a label when interpreting disagreements, rather than resolving them only through a vote.

The experiments report significantly better performance than commonly used approaches, including majority voting, without a significant increase in the computational cost of approximate Bayesian inference. The authors also propose an active learning methodology capable of further reducing annotation costs. Together, these contributions address both how to learn from heterogeneous annotations and how to obtain additional annotations more economically. The performance and computational findings are empirical results from the evaluated settings.
icml-2014-gaussian-process-classificatio.tldr: A Gaussian process classifier accounts for differing annotator expertise, with an active learning extension to reduce annotation cost.

paragraphs: The paper develops a solver for linear programming relaxations of maximum a posteriori, or MAP, inference. These relaxations are useful because the original inference problem is often intractable. Existing solver choices involve a tradeoff: efficient dual block-coordinate descent methods can stop at suboptimal points, while globally convergent subgradient approaches are often slower in practice.

Another approach computes a steepest epsilon-descent direction by solving a quadratic program. The authors build on this idea but use the Frank-Wolfe approach to decouple that quadratic program. This restructuring produces an efficient algorithm that is straightforward to parallelize while preserving global convergence.

The distinction between the relaxed and original problems matters: the convergence claim concerns solving the MAP linear programming relaxation. Experiments on spin-glass models and protein design tasks show superior performance over the compared algorithms. The contribution therefore joins a convergence property with a computational organization suitable for parallel execution, addressing the practical tension between reliable optimization and speed in this class of inference solvers.
icml-2014-globally-convergent-parallel-m.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe-based decomposition yields an easily parallelized MAP linear-programming relaxation solver with global convergence.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among data points to help predict classes when labels are only partially available. Smoothness expresses how predictions should relate across that graph. This paper focuses on combining two aspects of smoothness: its behavior at individual points and an explicit probabilistic formulation.

The authors introduce Probabilistic Graph-based Pointwise Smoothness, abbreviated PGP. Its construction starts from models of data closeness and label coupling. These address related but distinct questions: how data points are connected, and how their labels are linked. The framework combines them into probability constraints that support class prediction.

The contribution is a joint treatment of pointwise smoothness and probabilistic modeling, which the authors identify as absent from existing graph-based work. They provide theoretical analyses of prediction error and robustness, alongside extensive experiments reporting advantages for PGP. This gives the framework both an analytical treatment and empirical support. Its significance is to make the local meaning of smoothness part of the probability model used for prediction.
icml-2014-graph-based-semi-supervised-le.tldr: PGP combines pointwise smoothness and probability constraints to support graph-based semi-supervised classification.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiclass classification when different mistakes carry different costs. Its central concern is the loss function used to train the classifier. The authors argue that unreliable behavior in existing algorithms stems from losses that fail to enforce a basic preference for correct classification over arbitrary guessing.

They call this property guess-aversion. When a classifier gives all classes equal scores, it leaves the decision to an arbitrary guess. A guess-averse loss encourages correct classification over that outcome. Although the property holds trivially in binary classification, it does not automatically carry over when there are multiple classes.

The authors derive a family of cost-sensitive losses satisfying this property and use them to construct GEL-MCBoost and GLL-MCBoost. Extensive experiments support the importance of guess-aversion and show the GLL loss outperforming other evaluated losses for multiclass boosting. The practical message is that incorporating mistake costs is only part of loss design: how the loss treats an uninformative tie among classes also matters to the behavior of the resulting classifier.
icml-2014-guess-averse-loss-functions-fo.tldr: Guess-averse losses encourage correct predictions over equal-score guessing and underpin new cost-sensitive multiclass boosting algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a representation problem in scene recognition: low-level image features may not adequately explain high-level scene labels. A classifier therefore needs a useful connection between what the image measurements capture and what the output category means. The authors propose learning that connection through a patch-based latent variable model.

The model jointly trains a contextual representation and a classifier within one optimization framework. Its latent variables form an intermediate layer between input features and output labels. This layer has two linked requirements: it should help discriminate among semantic labels, and it should remain predictable from the low-level features available in the image.

Joint learning makes the representation's role in classification part of the training problem itself. The latent layer is useful insofar as it connects observable image information with the semantic distinctions the classifier must make. Experiments on standard scene recognition tasks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. These results provide empirical support for the proposed way of bridging low-level inputs and high-level outputs.
icml-2014-latent-semantic-representation.tldr: A jointly trained patch-based latent representation connects low-level image features with semantic scene labels.

paragraphs: This paper develops prediction algorithms for settings with both many training examples and many input dimensions. It covers multiclass prediction and multilabel prediction. The proposed algorithms are built around iterative least-squares updates and are described as robust and parameter free, offering a simple computational foundation for these large problems.

The authors present several variants with convergence guarantees. Their effectiveness is attributed to the use of second-order structure, which carries information beyond the first-order information used by gradient-based methods. The abstract reports substantial advantages over first-order methods in many practical scenarios, while keeping that comparison qualified rather than universal.

The empirical work shows how the approach scales to high-dimensional datasets. On MNIST and CIFAR-10, the authors report dramatic computational speedups over packages including Liblinear and Vowpal Wabbit while attaining state-of-the-art accuracies. These findings make the contribution about both optimization and prediction: the reported speed gains accompany strong predictive results. The paper thus revisits least-squares updates as a practical basis for scalable classification algorithms.
icml-2014-least-squares-revisited-scalab.tldr: Iterative least-squares algorithms exploit second-order structure to deliver scalable multiclass and multilabel prediction with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper considers control of Markov decision processes with large state spaces and an average-cost objective. Competing with the unrestricted optimal policy is treated as intractable at this scale. The authors instead aim to approach the best performance available within a low-dimensional comparison family of policies.

They use a dual linear programming formulation whose variable describes a stationary distribution over state-action pairs. State-action features define a low-dimensional subset of these distributions, and a neighborhood of that subset supplies the comparison class. This shifts the representation of the control problem toward a restricted family that can be handled computationally.

Two solution techniques are proposed: stochastic convex optimization and constraint sampling. For both, performance bounds approach the best achievable within the comparison class. Crucially, the stated results depend on the size of that class rather than the number of states. Preliminary experiments in a queuing application support the algorithms' effectiveness. The guarantee is therefore meaningful relative to the chosen family, without claiming competition with every possible policy.
icml-2014-linear-programming-for-large-s.tldr: Two linear-programming-based methods approach the best policy in a restricted comparison class with bounds independent of state-space size.

paragraphs: The paper presents a solver intended to make support vector machine training more practical on large datasets. It works with the primal SVM formulation, uses L2 regularization, and supports Lp loss functions. The optimization method is based on augmented Lagrange multipliers and is presented with a linear-time computational cost.

A central computational feature is that matrix-vector multiplication accounts for the most intensive steps determining the algorithm's complexity. These operations are straightforward to parallelize on a multicore server. The approach therefore connects its optimization formulation to a concrete kind of computation that can take advantage of parallel hardware.

The authors implement the solver within the interfaces and framework of LibLinear. Experiments report stable performance and faster average execution than evaluated solvers, including SVMperf, Pegasos, and LibLinear's TRON, PCD, and DCD implementations. The average qualification matters: the stated finding is a comparative empirical result, not a claim of winning every individual case. The contribution combines an SVM optimization method, a parallelizable computational core, and integration into an established software framework.
icml-2014-linear-time-solver-for-primal-.tldr: An augmented-Lagrangian primal SVM solver uses parallelizable matrix-vector operations and reports faster average performance than evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper studies interactive clustering under a practical restriction: each step may make only local changes to the current clustering. The algorithms can begin from any initial clustering. Together, these properties describe a process that improves an existing grouping incrementally, without requiring a specially prepared starting arrangement.

The theoretical question is whether these restrictions still permit efficient and accurate clustering. The authors show that they do for datasets satisfying the stability assumptions used in their analysis. Stability is therefore part of the setting supporting the result. The guarantee concerns datasets with that structure, rather than every possible collection of points.

The authors also report good performance on real-world data. This complements the theoretical result with empirical evidence for the algorithms' usefulness. The contribution establishes that arbitrary initialization and local updates can coexist with provable efficiency and accuracy under the stated assumptions. That combination matters for interactive workflows because the algorithm can work from a current clustering and revise it through a sequence of limited changes.
icml-2014-local-algorithms-for-interacti.tldr: Under stability assumptions, interactive clustering can start from any grouping and reach accurate results through efficient local changes.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo methods represent uncertainty using collections of particles. Memory becomes a serious concern when individual particles are large and many are needed, as in some high-dimensional latent-variable problems. Standard implementations require memory proportional to the particle count throughout the algorithm.

The authors propose a two-pass particle-generation scheme. During the first pass, particles are represented implicitly. The resulting memory cost depends on how many distinct particles survive resampling. This makes the storage requirement sensitive to the surviving particle collection rather than simply the full number generated.

The method also changes the user-facing resource choice: a memory budget replaces a fixed particle count. The algorithm adaptively selects an optimal number of particles to exploit that budget, and the authors show that this adaptation preserves the usual SMC consistency guarantees. Experiments report a large effect on approximation quality and running time in realistic scenarios. The timing benefit is connected to the cost of memory access, making memory management part of both statistical and computational efficiency.
icml-2014-memory-and-time-efficient-sequ.tldr: A two-pass SMC scheme adapts particle counts to a memory budget while preserving consistency and reducing storage demands.

paragraphs: This paper studies relational reinforcement learning when the agent is uncertain about which objects exist. Objects may appear or disappear depending on previous actions or properties of other objects. Achieving a goal can require actively discovering objects, so planning must consider potential objects that have not yet been observed.

An exact treatment generally leads to a partially observable Markov decision process, with beliefs about object existence and properties. The authors propose a computationally efficient approximation using discrete uncertainty predicates. Probabilistic rules learn how these approximate beliefs change, and an extension of existing planners supports planning in the resulting belief space.

The theoretical result connects the learned rules to the exact formulation: they encode an approximation of POMDP belief updates. Experiments show that the method learns relational rules appropriate for solving the studied problems. The contribution is therefore a representation and learning approach for object uncertainty, accompanied by a formal account of what its updates approximate. It enables discovery-related uncertainty to enter planning without claiming exact belief tracking.
icml-2014-model-based-relational-rl-when.tldr: Discrete uncertainty predicates and learned probabilistic rules enable approximate relational planning when objects may be undiscovered, appear, or disappear.

paragraphs: The paper introduces two neural language models that can condition language on another modality. Its main setting pairs images and text. In that setting, the models can support image retrieval from complex sentence queries, retrieval of phrase descriptions from image queries, and text generation conditioned on an image.

The authors show that word representations and image features can be learned jointly by training the language models together with a convolutional network. This places the visual and linguistic representations within a shared training process. The image representation participates in the language modeling task rather than being considered only as a separate input description.

A notable capability is generating sentence descriptions without templates, structured prediction, or syntactic trees. The contribution thus connects cross-modal retrieval with direct language generation through multimodal language modeling. Although the work focuses on images and text, the authors state that the algorithms can also be applied to modalities such as audio. That broader applicability is presented as an extension of the approach, rather than a reported audio experiment.
icml-2014-multimodal-neural-language-mod.tldr: Two multimodal neural language models support image-text retrieval and template-free image descriptions through jointly learned visual and word representations.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to train structural support vector machines that tolerate perturbations in their feature space. Earlier binary SVM analysis had connected robustness with regularization. The authors extend this line of reasoning to structured prediction, formulating robust learning problems for two classes of allowable perturbations.

For ellipsoidal uncertainty sets, the robust problem is equivalent to adding a regularizer based on the dual norm associated with the uncertainty constraint. For polyhedral sets, the equivalent addition is a linear regularizer in a transformed weight space related to the polyhedron's constraints. These results make the shape of the assumed perturbations directly relevant to the regularizer used in training.

The authors also show how the constraint sets can be combined and examine special cases. Experiments on real-world data report improvements over nonrobust structural SVMs when the test distribution has drifted from the training distribution. The theoretical contribution is the equivalence between specified robustness formulations and regularization; the empirical contribution supports their usefulness under the evaluated distribution shifts.
icml-2014-on-robustness-and-regularizati.tldr: Specified feature-perturbation models for structural SVMs are equivalent to additional regularizers, with empirical benefits under distribution shift.

paragraphs: The paper connects graph layout and vector embedding, two approaches to arranging data in two or three dimensions. The authors prove optimization equivalences linking beta with gamma divergences and alpha with Renyi divergences through a connection scalar. These relationships allow methods from the two traditions to be understood within a common framework.

That framework is generalized stochastic neighbor embedding, which compares similarities in the original data with similarities in the displayed layout. The optimal connection scalar supplies a natural balance between attractive and repulsive forces. The equivalences therefore serve both as a theoretical connection and as a way to construct visualization methods.

The authors demonstrate this with two developments. Weighted symmetric stochastic neighbor embedding, derived from Elastic Embedding, performs well across tested vector and network datasets, while comparison methods fail on some datasets. A gamma-divergence version of PolyLog layout is scale invariant in the output space and permits efficient use of large-scale smoothed neighborhoods. These examples show how the equivalences yield concrete algorithmic properties and empirical benefits.
icml-2014-optimization-equivalence-of-di.tldr: Optimization equivalences between divergences connect graph layout with neighbor embedding and enable new visualization methods.

paragraphs: The paper accelerates support vector machine training by removing examples that cannot affect the resulting classifier. Its starting point is that non-support vectors have no effect on the solution. The authors derive screening rules, called DVI, by analyzing the SVM dual problem through variational inequalities.

The key property is safety: every discarded vector is guaranteed to be a non-support vector. Screening therefore reduces the optimization dataset without changing the classifier through an incorrect removal. The procedure needs one scan of the dataset, has a cost described as negligible relative to solving the SVM problem, and can be combined with any existing efficient solver.

The technique also extends to identifying non-support vectors in least absolute deviations regression. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report stronger screening performance than existing SVM screening rules and effective removal for regression. Reported speedups reach up to two orders of magnitude. This is an upper-end observed gain, while the broader contribution is a solver-independent route to exact data reduction for both learning problems.
icml-2014-scaling-svm-and-least-absolute.tldr: Safe screening rules remove irrelevant training examples before SVM or least absolute deviations optimization, with reported speedups up to two orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: The paper proposes two algorithms for sparse reinforcement learning, using different optimization formulations. The pair addresses offline and online computation. Its organizing idea is that the learning problem can be approached through convex optimization tools, with the formulation determining how the relevant error and regularization are handled.

The offline algorithm uses the alternating direction method of multipliers. It solves a constrained problem that explicitly controls the projected Bellman residual, a measure of mismatch in the projected value-learning relation. The online algorithm instead uses stochastic approximation with regularized dual averaging, working from a Lagrangian formulation of the problem.

The authors establish convergence for both algorithms and demonstrate their performance on two classical examples. This supplies theoretical support for both computational approaches alongside illustrative empirical evidence. The contribution is the combination of two formulations and corresponding solvers: one makes residual control explicit through a constraint, while the other supports online updates through its stochastic approximation scheme. The stated findings establish convergence and demonstrate performance without asserting universal superiority for either algorithm.
icml-2014-sparse-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: Two convergent sparse reinforcement learning algorithms use constrained offline optimization and regularized online stochastic approximation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a network will respond to a particular action. The output is a subnetwork identifying both the nodes that perform the action and the directed edges that relay it. This treats the response as a connected prediction problem involving node activity and directed transmission.

The proposed method, SPIN, uses max-margin structured learning to score compatibility between actions and activated subnetworks. Influence is context-sensitive: its presence, direction, and dynamics depend on the action's properties. The model can therefore represent different network responses to different actions through the learned compatibility score.

The authors prove that finding the highest-scoring network and the worst margin-violating network are NP-hard inference problems. They provide an approximate method based on semidefinite programming relaxation and a more scalable greedy heuristic. Experiments show markedly better predictive performance than competing methods when action context and network structure are used. The contribution combines a context-dependent response model with practical approximate inference procedures for its computationally difficult prediction and training tasks.
icml-2014-structured-prediction-of-netwo.tldr: SPIN predicts action-dependent network responses through structured learning, using approximate inference for the resulting NP-hard problems.
